title: Regulation of Multinational Banks: A Theoretical Inquiry
summary_en: How should regulators handle banks operating across multiple countries — through subsidiaries, branches, or cross-border lending? Calzolari and Lóránth model the choice of supervisory architecture (home-country vs. host-country supervision) when banks face deposit-insurance and capital-requirement rules in each jurisdiction. They characterise when host-country supervision dominates (information advantages) vs. home-country (avoidance of duplicative compliance), and identify the deposit-insurance design that aligns each model's incentives.
data_used: Theoretical paper. No primary dataset; the analysis is a contract-theoretic model of multi-jurisdictional banking supervision.
policy_relevance: Useful theoretical input for European Banking Union debates and for the MNB's role within the SSM (Single Supervisory Mechanism): the paper formalises why the SSM's hybrid home-host-supervisor structure can dominate either pure regime, and identifies the deposit-insurance design (EDIS) needed to align incentives. Directly relevant for Hungarian central-bank decisions about euro adoption and full SSM participation.
